content: Pyogenic sterile arthritis, pyoderma gangrenosum, and acne syndrome, also known as PAPA syndrome, is a rare inherited autoinflammatory disorder. It is characterized by a triad of aseptic arthritis, pyoderma gangrenosum, and acne. However, not all patients exhibit all three features. PAPA syndrome was first identified in 1997 by Dr. Noralane M. Lindor after observing similar clinical presentations in three generations of a single family. In 2000, a mutation in the PSTPIP1 gene was linked to the syndrome. This mutation is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner and results in a hyper-phosphorylated PSTPIP1 protein, which alters its role in the inflammasome responsible for interleukin-1 beta (IL-1β) production. Overproduction of IL-1β is a hallmark molecular feature of PAPA syndrome. The syndrome must be differentiated from other conditions that cause arthritis, skin rashes, and pyoderma gangrenosum, such as Blau syndrome, familial cold autoinflammatory syndrome, chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis (CRMO), and juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA). PAPA syndrome is rare, with an estimated prevalence of 1 case per 100,000 individuals worldwide. To date, 53 cases have been reported in the literature. It typically affects children but can manifest later in life. There is no racial predilection, and it affects males and females equally. Most cases have been reported in Europe, New Zealand, and the USA. The natural history of PAPA syndrome often begins with arthritis symptoms between the ages of 1 and 10 years. Skin lesions, which usually affect the limbs, tend to develop later during adolescence. The disease exhibits variable expressivity and incomplete penetrance. Common complications include erosive arthritis, and the severity of the disease often decreases with age. However, serious joint destruction may occur in some cases. Prognostic data for PAPA syndrome are currently unavailable. Diagnosis of PAPA syndrome is primarily clinical, as there are no established diagnostic criteria. Genetic analysis to identify mutations in the PSTPIP1 gene can confirm the diagnosis, but some cases with negative genetic results have been reported. A history of recurrent arthritis, skin ulceration, and acne is suggestive of the syndrome. The presenting symptom is often culture-negative arthritis. Physical examination findings include arthritis, cystic acne, pathergy, and pyoderma gangrenosum. Fever may accompany disease flares. Laboratory findings consistent with PAPA syndrome include elevated serum levels of C-reactive protein (CRP), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), and white blood cell (WBC) count. Skin lesions and joint fluid are sterile, but synovial fluid typically shows a neutrophilic infiltrate. Elevated levels of tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) and interleukin-1 have been observed in the blood of affected individuals. Imaging studies, such as X-rays, MRI, and CT scans, do not reveal specific findings associated with PAPA syndrome. However, they may help identify complications of arthritis, such as soft tissue swelling, joint effusion, synovitis, synovial hypertrophy, bone marrow edema, and joint destruction. There are no findings on electrocardiography, echocardiography, or ultrasound specific to PAPA syndrome. There is no definitive treatment for PAPA syndrome, and management is primarily supportive. Intra-articular corticosteroid injections may be used for arthritis, while oral corticosteroids can be effective for pyoderma gangrenosum. Anakinra, an interleukin-1 antagonist, has shown efficacy in managing disease flares, particularly articular symptoms. Adalimumab, a tumor necrosis factor antagonist, may be effective for cutaneous manifestations. Surgical intervention is not recommended for managing PAPA syndrome. There are no established measures for the primary or secondary prevention of PAPA syndrome. Routine screening is not recommended due to insufficient evidence.
